title: What you need
description: What Flexarr is, what kind of computer can run it, and whether you need Sonarr, Radarr, Lidarr and the other *arr apps.
headings: Do you need Sonarr, Radarr and Lidarr?
text: Flexarr comes in two halves. The server runs on a computer in your home and keeps your films, TV shows, music and podcasts. The apps on your iPhone, iPad, Apple TV and web browser connect to it and play from it. There's no account and no cloud service in the middle: your library stays on your own disk. If you've installed the iPhone app and it sent you here, this is the part you're missing. Set up the server once, then connect your phone to it with a short code. Flexarr is free for personal and other noncommercial use under the PolyForm Noncommercial licence. #A computer that stays on The server needs a machine that's switched on whenever you want to watch. Any of these work: A Mac, Apple silicon or Intel. Flexarr runs on it natively and uses the Mac's graphics chip to convert video. A NAS that runs containers, such as a Synology or an Unraid server. A Linux box or mini PC with Docker. That includes a Raspberry Pi 5 running a 64-bit operating system. A Windows PC with Docker Desktop. The Docker image is built for both 64-bit Intel/AMD (amd64) and 64-bit ARM (arm64) processors. There's no 32-bit build, and no native Windows or Linux download: on those, Docker is the way in. #Disk space Your media takes whatever it takes. Flexarr itself needs room for its database and a cache of artwork, subtitles, scrubbing previews and video it's converting at the moment. Leave a few gigabytes free on the drive that holds Flexarr's settings folder, more for a large library. #Processor and hardware transcoding Most of the time Flexarr sends files as they are. The iPhone, iPad and Apple TV apps play files directly by default, HDR and Dolby Vision included, so the server does little more than read from disk. The server converts (transcodes) video when a device can't play a file as it is: a web browser meeting a format it doesn't know, a stream limited to a lower quality for watching away from home, or some downloads. Converting is hard work for a processor, so this is where the machine matters: On a Mac, Flexarr uses Apple VideoToolbox automatically. Any recent Mac copes well. In Docker, Flexarr converts on the processor unless you choose hardware acceleration in Settings › Streaming, which lists only what the server's FFmpeg supports. See your platform's install page for what's available there. A modest machine is fine if you mostly watch on Apple devices at home. If you plan to stream to browsers or over a slow connection a lot, a faster processor (or a Mac) helps. Flexarr converts at most three videos at once by default and tells anyone beyond that the server is busy, rather than slowing everybody down. #Do you need Sonarr, Radarr and Lidarr? Flexarr is built to sit alongside Sonarr (TV), Radarr (films), Lidarr (music) and Seerr (requests). It doesn't download anything itself, and it takes its titles, artwork and details from those apps rather than asking you for API keys to online databases. You can run Flexarr without them, but what you get differs by library. Library With the app Without it Films Radarr supplies titles, posters, backgrounds, overviews, genres, ratings, trailers and cast. Films Radarr doesn't manage are looked up through its search. Films are found and play, named from their folders and files. Artwork and details come from any .nfo file and images (poster.jpg, fanart.jpg) in the film's folder, or from TMDB with a free key of your own. TV shows Sonarr supplies show and episode details and artwork. Flexarr adds cast from TVmaze. Episodes are found and play, organised from names like S01E02. Artwork and details come from any tvshow.nfo, episode .nfo files and images (poster.jpg, season01-poster.jpg, -thumb.jpg) beside them, or from TVmaze, which needs no setup. Music Lidarr adds artist pictures, album details and sorts albums, EPs and singles apart. Works well: Flexarr reads the tags in your files and uses cover.jpg or folder.jpg images, or art embedded in the files. Audiobooks (in the next release) Readarr, Bookshelf or Chaptarr fetch books, add details and covers, and let you request books. Works well: Flexarr reads the folders, tags and files beside each book, and looks up what's missing on Audible and Open Library. Requests Seerr lets you search for and request films and shows from any of the apps. No requests. Subtitles Bazarr lets you search for subtitles from the player, and re-sync ones that are out of time. Subtitles in or beside your files only. A few other things depend on the *arrs too: New downloads appear straight away when Sonarr, Radarr or Lidarr tell Flexarr about them with a webhook, which Flexarr adds to each app for you. Without that, Flexarr finds new files on its own scan, every 12 hours, or when you start one in Settings › Libraries. Coming soon, showing episodes about to air and films about to be released, comes from Sonarr and Radarr (and, in the next release, books on the way from Readarr). Some features don't need any of them: podcasts are built in, Live TV uses Dispatcharr, and the web app, profiles, downloads to your phone and importing your history from Plex all work on their own. Tip If you don't run the *arrs yet, you can start with Flexarr and a folder of media, then add Sonarr and Radarr later. Flexarr tries unmatched titles again within a day, or straight away when you choose Refresh artwork and details on a library in Settings › Libraries. Note Seerr only adds requests. Flexarr talks to Sonarr, Radarr and Lidarr directly for everything else. #The apps iPhone and iPad: on the App Store. Apple TV: coming soon to the App Store. Until then you can install it from Xcode. Web: built into the server. Open the server's address in any browser. Android and Android TV apps are on the way: see flexarr.io/apps. #Pick your platform Install on a Mac Install on a Synology NAS Install on Unraid Install with Docker on Linux or Windows

title: Install on a Mac
description: Build Flexarr from source and run it natively on a Mac as a background service, with hardware video conversion through VideoToolbox.
headings: If your *arrs run in Docker on this Mac
text: On a Mac, Flexarr runs natively rather than in Docker. That way it can use the Mac's graphics hardware (Apple VideoToolbox) to convert video, which Docker on macOS can't. It works on Apple silicon and Intel Macs. A Mac app is coming to the Mac App Store. Until then, you build Flexarr from its source code with one command, which installs it as a background service that starts when you log in. It takes some time in Terminal, but you only do it once. Note Prefer not to build anything? Docker Desktop for Mac runs the Docker image too, but without VideoToolbox: video is converted on the processor. #Before you start You'll build on one Mac and install on another over SSH. They can be the same Mac, which is what this page assumes. You need: macOS command line tools (git, make, Python). Run xcode-select --install in Terminal, or install Xcode. Homebrew, for FFmpeg and Node.js. The .NET 10 SDK, from Microsoft's download page. Choose the latest SDK installer for your Mac (Arm64 for Apple silicon, x64 for Intel). Node.js 24 or later: brew install node. FFmpeg, on the Mac that will run Flexarr: brew install ffmpeg. Flexarr uses it to read your files and convert video. #Turn on Remote Login The install script copies Flexarr into place and starts it over SSH, even on the same Mac. Open System Settings › General › Sharing and turn on Remote Login. In Terminal, make an SSH key if you don't have one, and let it sign in to this Mac without a password: ssh-keygen -t ed25519 # press Return to accept the defaults ssh-copy-id localhost ssh localhost true # should finish without asking for a password #Build and install Get the source code of the latest release: git clone https://github.com/danleach-glitch/flexarr.git cd flexarr git checkout "$(git tag --list 'v*' --sort=-v:refname | head -1)" Build a release, not the newest code on main: that's work in progress, and once it has changed your database you can't go back to a release. Build and install: make deploy DEPLOY_HOST=localhost The script builds the web app and the server, downloads Microsoft's ASP.NET Core runtime into ~/.dotnet (checking it against Microsoft's published checksum), copies Flexarr into ~/.flexarr, and starts it. It waits until Flexarr answers, then prints its address, something like http://your-mac.local:8383, and on a new server a Set it up link with the setup code filled in. To install on a different Mac, use its SSH host name in place of localhost, for example make deploy DEPLOY_HOST=mini. That Mac needs Remote Login and FFmpeg, but not the SDK or Node.js. #Where things live Path What's there ~/.flexarr/app Flexarr itself. Replaced each time you install. ~/.flexarr/data Your settings (config.json), database and caches. Installing never touches it. ~/.flexarr/logs Log files, one a day. console.log has errors from when the server couldn't start. ~/Library/LaunchAgents/io.github.flexarr.server.plist The service: starts Flexarr at login and restarts it if it stops. #Keep it running Flexarr runs as a LaunchAgent, which means it runs while you're logged in. On a Mac that acts as a server: Turn on automatic login for your user in System Settings › Users & Groups. (macOS doesn't offer it while FileVault is on.) Stop the Mac going to sleep on its own, in System Settings' energy or battery settings. To restart, stop or start Flexarr by hand: launchctl kickstart -k gui/$(id -u)/io.github.flexarr.server # restart launchctl bootout gui/$(id -u)/io.github.flexarr.server # stop launchctl bootstrap gui/$(id -u) ~/Library/LaunchAgents/io.github.flexarr.server.plist # start #Media on an external drive The first time Flexarr reads a library on an external drive, macOS may ask whether to allow access. Allow it. If scans can't see your media, look in System Settings › Privacy & Security under Files & Folders (or Full Disk Access) for dotnet, the program Flexarr runs under, and turn its access on. #Hardware transcoding Nothing to set up. Settings › Streaming › Hardware acceleration starts on Automatic, which on a Mac means Apple VideoToolbox. The graphics hardware decodes H.264 and HEVC; other formats (older AVI files, VC-1 and the like) are decoded on the processor and still encoded in hardware. #If your *arrs run in Docker on this Mac Sonarr, Radarr and Lidarr in Docker see your media under their own paths, such as /data/tv. Flexarr usually works out where those are on the Mac by itself; Settings › Connections › Media folders shows what it found, and lets you choose any it couldn't. From inside a container, the Mac is host.docker.internal, so webhooks go to http://host.docker.internal:8383. Connect Sonarr, Radarr and Lidarr and Media paths cover both. #Updating The easiest way is Update now in Settings › Updates. Or check out the newest release and install again. Your settings and library stay as they are. cd flexarr git fetch --tags git checkout "$(git tag --list 'v*' --sort=-v:refname | head -1)" make deploy DEPLOY_HOST=localhost See Updating for more. #Next: set it up Open the Set it up link the install printed, and choose a PIN: the code is already filled in. Without the link, open http://your-mac.local:8383 (or http://localhost:8383 on the Mac itself) and enter the setup code from ~/.flexarr/data/setup-code.txt. The first browser with the code becomes the new server's owner. Carry on with First setup.

title: Install on a Synology NAS
description: Run Flexarr on a Synology NAS as a Container Manager project, with its settings folder, your media and the right permissions.
text: On a Synology NAS, Flexarr runs as a container in Container Manager, Synology's Docker app. You need DSM 7.2 or later and a model that supports Container Manager. Flexarr's image is built for both Intel/AMD and 64-bit ARM processors, so if Container Manager installs on your model, Flexarr should run. #1. Install Container Manager Open Package Center, search for Container Manager and install it. Installing it creates a shared folder called docker. #2. Make the folders Container Manager won't create missing folders for you, so make them first in File Station: In the docker shared folder, create a folder called flexarr. Inside it, create a folder called config. This holds Flexarr's settings, database and caches. Note where your media is, for example /volume1/data/media with movies, tv and music inside. If you run Sonarr, Radarr and Lidarr on the NAS, use the folder they use. #3. Find your user ID You tell the Flexarr container which user to run as, with PUID and PGID, so it can write to its folder and read your media. You need that user's numeric ID and group ID. In Control Panel › Terminal & SNMP, tick Enable SSH service and apply. From a computer, connect with ssh yourname@your-nas and run id: id # uid=1026(yourname) gid=100(users) ... Note the two numbers (here 1026 and 100). You can turn SSH off again afterwards. Tip Use an account that can read your media shares and write to the docker share. If your *arrs already run with a PUID and PGID, use those same numbers. #4. Create the project Open Container Manager and go to Project, then Create. Project name: flexarr. Path: choose Set path and pick docker/flexarr. Source: choose Create docker-compose.yml and paste this, changing the IDs and the media path to yours: services: flexarr: image: ghcr.io/danleach-glitch/flexarr:latest container_name: flexarr environment: [PUID=1026, PGID=100] ports: ["8383:8383"] volumes: - /volume1/docker/flexarr/config:/config - /volume1/data/media:/data/media restart: unless-stopped Click Next. You can skip the web portal settings. Click Next again, then Done. Container Manager downloads the image and starts Flexarr. The project shows as running when it's ready. #About the media path Mount your media at the same path inside the container that Sonarr, Radarr and Lidarr use inside theirs. If they all see /data/media/tv/..., the paths they report to Flexarr match what Flexarr sees and everything lines up. If they don't, you can map one to the other in Settings › Connections › Media folders. See Media paths. #Port Flexarr listens on port 8383. If you use DSM's firewall (Control Panel › Security › Firewall), allow that port from your home network. #Hardware transcoding Flexarr converts video on the processor by default. Many Intel-based Synology models have a graphics chip that can do this work, and the Flexarr image includes the Intel drivers. If your NAS has /dev/dri (check with ls /dev/dri over SSH), add this to the service in the project's docker-compose.yml: devices: - /dev/dri:/dev/dri Then choose Intel Quick Sync or VA-API (Intel and AMD on Linux) in Settings › Streaming › Hardware acceleration and play something that needs converting. If it fails, set it back to Automatic. This matters less than you might expect: the iPhone, iPad and Apple TV apps play most files directly, so the server only converts for web browsers, quality-limited streams away from home and some downloads. On a NAS with a low-power processor, keep those to one or two at a time. #Updating When a new release is out, Container Manager's Image page marks the Flexarr image as having an update. Select it and choose Update, and Container Manager restarts Flexarr on the new version. Your settings stay in docker/flexarr/config. See Updating. #Next: set it up In Container Manager, select the container and open Log. It says Set it up at http://localhost:8383/#setup=…. Copy that link into a browser on your home network, putting the NAS's name or IP address in place of localhost. The page has the setup code filled in, so you only choose a PIN. The first browser to do it becomes the new server's owner. Carry on with First setup.

title: Install on Unraid
description: Add Flexarr to Unraid as a Docker container by hand, with its appdata folder, your media share and the right user.
text: On Unraid, Flexarr runs as a Docker container. There's no Community Applications template for it yet, so you add the container by hand. It takes a few minutes and you only do it once. #Before you start Make sure Docker is enabled, under Settings › Docker. Know where your media lives, for example the data share at /mnt/user/data/media. If you run Sonarr, Radarr and Lidarr on this server, look at the media path in their containers' settings: you'll give Flexarr the same one. #Add the container Go to the Docker tab and click Add Container at the bottom of the page. Fill in the top of the form: Name: flexarr Repository: ghcr.io/danleach-glitch/flexarr:latest Network Type: Host, so the Apple TV and iPhone apps find Flexarr by themselves. Bridge works too, but then you type the server's address in the apps. Switch the form to the advanced view with the Basic View toggle at the top right, and fill in: WebUI: http://[IP]:[PORT:8383]/ Add the port, the settings folder, your media and the user to run as with Add another Path, Port, Variable, Label or Device at the bottom, one at a time: Config Type Name Container Host Port Web UI 8383 8383 Path Config /config /mnt/user/appdata/flexarr Path Media /data/media /mnt/user/data/media Variable PUID PUID 99 Variable PGID PGID 100 Change the media paths to match yours. The container path should be the one your *arrs use inside their containers. With Network Type Host, leave out the Port row: Flexarr is at port 8383 on the server itself. Click Apply. Unraid downloads the image and starts Flexarr. #Why PUID 99 and PGID 100 They run Flexarr as Unraid's usual nobody:users, the owner of files on your shares and in appdata, so it can write its settings and read your media. If your other containers use a different PUID and PGID, use those numbers instead. Flexarr gives appdata/flexarr to that user when it starts. #Media paths Sonarr, Radarr and Lidarr tell Flexarr where each new file is. When all of them see your media at the same container path (here /data/media), those paths match and new downloads appear straight away. If they don't, map one to the other in Settings › Connections › Media folders. See Media paths. #Hardware transcoding Flexarr converts video on the processor by default. On Linux, Settings › Streaming › Hardware acceleration › Automatic means the processor. Intel and AMD graphics. The image includes the drivers. Edit the container and add a Device with /dev/dri as its value, then apply. VA-API (Intel and AMD on Linux), and on Intel Intel Quick Sync, appear in Settings › Streaming. Choose one and play something that needs converting. If it fails, set it back to Automatic. NVIDIA graphics may work, because Unraid's NVIDIA driver supplies the libraries to the container. This is untested, so treat it as an experiment: Install the Nvidia Driver plugin from the Apps tab and reboot if it asks. Edit the Flexarr container. Add --runtime=nvidia to Extra Parameters. Add two Variables: NVIDIA_VISIBLE_DEVICES set to all (or your card's ID from the plugin's page), and NVIDIA_DRIVER_CAPABILITIES set to compute,video,utility. Apply, then choose NVIDIA NVENC in Settings › Streaming and play something that needs converting. If it fails, set it back to Automatic. Note Conversion matters less than you might think. The iPhone, iPad and Apple TV apps play most files directly, so the server mainly converts for web browsers, quality-limited streams away from home and some downloads. #Updating The Docker tab shows when a newer Flexarr image is available. Click apply update under the container to move to it. Your settings stay in appdata/flexarr. See Updating. #Next: set it up Click Flexarr's icon in the Docker tab and choose Logs. It says Set it up at http://localhost:8383/#setup=…. Copy that link into a browser on your home network, putting your Unraid server's name or IP address in place of localhost. The page has the setup code filled in, so you only choose a PIN and choose Set up Flexarr: the first browser to do it becomes the new server's owner. (Opening WebUI instead works too; then type the code from the log.) Carry on with First setup.

title: Install with Docker on Linux or Windows
description: Run Flexarr's Docker image on a Linux machine, or on Windows through Docker Desktop and WSL 2, with docker run or Docker Compose.
text: On Linux and Windows, Flexarr runs as a Docker container. The image is ghcr.io/danleach-glitch/flexarr, built for 64-bit Intel/AMD (amd64) and 64-bit ARM (arm64), so it also runs on a Raspberry Pi 5 with a 64-bit operating system. There's no native Windows build: on Windows, use Docker Desktop. #What the container needs Inside the container What to give it Port 8383 Publish it as 8383 on the host. Settings /config A folder (or Docker volume) for Flexarr's settings, database and caches. Keep it: it's your whole setup. Media /data/media (your choice) Your media folder. Mount it at the same path Sonarr, Radarr and Lidarr use, so the paths they report match what Flexarr sees. The latest tag is always the newest release. To upgrade only when you choose, use a version instead, such as ghcr.io/danleach-glitch/flexarr:0.57. See Which tag to use. #Linux #Permissions Flexarr runs as user ID 1654 unless you tell it otherwise. It needs to write to its settings folder and read your media, so the simplest way is to run it as the user who owns your media with PUID and PGID, as with Sonarr, Radarr and Lidarr. Find your IDs with id: id # uid=1000(you) gid=1000(you) ... When it starts, Flexarr gives its settings folder to that user, so it doesn't matter if Docker created the folder as root. Note Docker's --user option (user: in Compose) works too, in place of PUID and PGID. The container then changes no owners, so create the settings folder yourself first (mkdir -p ~/flexarr/config) so it belongs to you. #docker run docker run -d --name flexarr --restart unless-stopped \ -e PUID=1000 -e PGID=1000 \ -p 8383:8383 \ -v ~/flexarr/config:/config \ -v /path/to/media:/data/media \ ghcr.io/danleach-glitch/flexarr:latest Tip You can keep the settings in a named Docker volume instead, with -v flexarr-config:/config. #Docker Compose Save this as docker-compose.yml and run docker compose up -d in the same folder. services: flexarr: image: ghcr.io/danleach-glitch/flexarr:latest container_name: flexarr environment: [PUID=1000, PGID=1000] ports: ["8383:8383"] volumes: - ./config:/config - /path/to/media:/data/media restart: unless-stopped If Sonarr, Radarr and Lidarr are in the same Compose file, give them the same media mount (/path/to/media:/data/media). They can then reach Flexarr at http://flexarr:8383 for webhooks. #Found on your network The Apple TV, iPhone and iPad list servers that announce themselves on the Wi-Fi. Docker's own network doesn't pass the announcement on, so to have Flexarr listed, run it on the host's network: --network host in place of -p 8383:8383 with docker run, or in Compose: network_mode: host in place of the ports: line. Flexarr is then at port 8383 on the computer itself. Without it, everything still works; in the apps, choose Enter an address instead and type http://<server>:8383. Note On the host's network, other containers in the Compose file can't reach Flexarr as http://flexarr:8383. Use the computer's address instead, or http://host.docker.internal:8383 with extra_hosts: ["host.docker.internal:host-gateway"] on those containers. #Hardware transcoding Flexarr converts video on the processor unless you pick something else in Settings › Streaming › Hardware acceleration. On Linux, Automatic means the processor. The menu lists only what the container can use. The Apple apps play most files directly, so many homes rarely need conversion at all. Intel and AMD graphics. The image includes the VA-API drivers: AMD's on both amd64 and arm64, Intel's (with Quick Sync) on amd64 only. Pass the graphics device into the container, with --device /dev/dri for docker run or this under the service in Compose: devices: - /dev/dri:/dev/dri Flexarr joins the device's group by itself. Then VA-API (Intel and AMD on Linux), and on Intel Intel Quick Sync, appear in Settings › Streaming. Choose one and play something that needs converting. If it fails, set it back to Automatic. Note With --user in place of PUID, Flexarr can't join the device's group by itself. Add it with --group-add (group_add: in Compose), using the group number from ls -n /dev/dri. NVIDIA works too, because the NVIDIA Container Toolkit supplies the driver libraries to the container. With the toolkit installed on the host, add runtime: nvidia to the service in Compose, and two variables to its environment: list: runtime: nvidia environment: [PUID=1000, PGID=1000, NVIDIA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=all, "NVIDIA_DRIVER_CAPABILITIES=compute,video,utility"] With docker run, that's --runtime nvidia -e NVIDIA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=all -e NVIDIA_DRIVER_CAPABILITIES=compute,video,utility. Then choose NVIDIA NVENC in Settings › Streaming and play something that needs converting. If it fails, set it back to Automatic. #Windows Install Docker Desktop and keep its default WSL 2 backend. It asks to install WSL if you don't have it. In Docker Desktop's settings, turn on Start Docker Desktop when you sign in, so Flexarr comes back after a restart. Make a folder, say C:\flexarr, and save this in it as docker-compose.yml: services: flexarr: image: ghcr.io/danleach-glitch/flexarr:latest container_name: flexarr ports: ["8383:8383"] volumes: - flexarr-config:/config - D:/Media:/data/media restart: unless-stopped volumes: flexarr-config: Change D:/Media to where your media is, with forward slashes. Open PowerShell in that folder and run docker compose up -d. The apps don't find a server in Docker Desktop by themselves. In the app, choose Enter an address instead and type the PC's IP address, such as http://192.168.1.20:8383. If nothing connects, check that Windows' firewall lets other devices reach port 8383. #Performance on Windows Docker Desktop runs Linux containers inside WSL 2. Files on your Windows drives (C:, D:, which WSL sees as /mnt/c, /mnt/d) are reached across a bridge between Windows and Linux, which is much slower than Linux's own disk. Playback is usually fine, but library scans are slower, and a database there is slow and can be unreliable. That's why the Compose file above keeps /config in a Docker volume (flexarr-config), which lives inside WSL 2, and only your media on a Windows drive. Don't change /config to a folder like C:\flexarr\config. Note Your media can stay on any Windows drive, including a second internal disk. A network share mapped to a drive letter usually isn't visible to containers this way. If your media is on a NAS, consider running Flexarr on the NAS itself. #Hardware transcoding on Windows Flexarr converts on the processor. Docker Desktop can pass an NVIDIA graphics card through to containers, so the NVIDIA steps above may work, with gpus: all under the service in place of runtime: nvidia. Intel and AMD graphics aren't available to containers on Windows. #Next: set it up Look at the container's log (docker logs flexarr, or Logs on the container in Docker Desktop). It says This server isn't set up yet. Set it up at http://localhost:8383/#setup=…. Open that link: on the computer running Docker it works as it is, and from another computer put the server's name or IP address in place of localhost. The page has the setup code filled in, so you only choose a PIN. The first browser to do it becomes the new server's owner. Carry on with First setup.

title: First setup
description: Open your new Flexarr server in a browser, make yourself its owner, add your films, shows and music, and find the API key if you ever need it.
text: Once the server is installed and running, everything else happens in a web browser. There's no account to make and no key to copy: the first browser on your home network to enter the server's setup code becomes its owner. #Open Flexarr in a browser Flexarr listens on port 8383. On a computer on the same home network as the server, open: http://<server>:8383 Replace <server> with the server's address. Any of these usually work: On the server itself: http://localhost:8383 The server's name on your network, such as http://mac-mini.local:8383 Its IP address, such as http://192.168.1.20:8383. Your router's app or admin page lists the addresses of devices on your network. If the page doesn't load, check that Flexarr is running (your install guide, linked from What you need, shows how) and that you've typed http://, not https://. #Enter the setup code A new server greets you with Welcome to your Flexarr server. The setup code proves you're the one who installed it: some setups (a reverse proxy, Docker Desktop) make visitors from the internet look as though they're on your home network, and only someone with the server can read its code. It's eight letters and numbers, like K7QM-3PXT. Usually there's nothing to type, because the server gives you a link with the code filled in: Docker (including Synology and Unraid): the container's log (docker logs flexarr, or the log in your NAS's Docker app) says Set it up at http://localhost:8383/#setup=…. Open that link. From another computer, put the server's name or IP address in place of localhost. The code alone is in setup-code.txt in the container's settings folder. macOS (installed with the script): the script ends with a Set it up link. The code is also in ~/.flexarr/logs/console.log and ~/.flexarr/data/setup-code.txt. The Mac app (coming to the Mac App Store) opens the welcome page with the code filled in. Opened without the link, the page asks for the code and says where it is for your kind of install. Pasting the whole link into the Setup code box works too. Then choose the admin PIN (4 to 8 digits, typed twice). It protects the server's settings: watching doesn't need it; changing settings does. Choose Set up Flexarr. This browser becomes the server's owner and is signed in. That's the whole sign-up. If you close the page before choosing Set up Flexarr, nothing has happened yet, and the same code still works. The code stops working once the server is set up, and after ten wrong tries it's replaced with a new one (the log says so). A few things to know: It only works once. As soon as anyone signs in, setup closes for good. Phones, tablets and TVs then connect with a code that you allow from your phone or this browser (see Connect your devices). Other browsers sign in with the API key. It only works from home. The button appears only to a browser on your home network, reaching the server by its IP address, a .local name or the server's own name. That stops anyone on the internet, or a web page you happen to visit, from claiming your server. Older servers don't need any of this. One set up before version 0.49.0 keeps using the API key, and one without an admin PIN asks you to Choose an admin PIN the first time you open Settings. Note If you see a box asking for an API key instead of the welcome, someone has already set this server up, or you're not on the home network. Try opening it by its IP address from a computer at home. If you set it up yourself in another browser, sign in here with the key (see The API key below). #The setup guide Next, Flexarr welcomes you with a short setup guide, one card at a time. Choose Get started, or I'll set it up myself to go straight to Home. Every step after your name can be skipped, and Set up later leaves the guide whenever you like: What's your name? Type your name and choose a colour for your profile, the one that runs Flexarr. Connect your apps. Connect Sonarr, Radarr and Lidarr (and, in the next release, Readarr), if you use them. If Flexarr finds one running nearby, its address is filled in already, and you only paste its API key. Flexarr also adds its own webhook to each app in the background (Setting up instant updates…), so new downloads show up straight away (see Webhooks). Connected the wrong one? Choose Disconnect. Don't use them? Choose Skip. Add your libraries. There's a line each for Movies, TV Shows and Music (and Audiobooks, in the next release, when Readarr is connected). A folder from Sonarr, Radarr or Lidarr is filled in already. Otherwise choose Choose folder, go to the folder that holds it and choose Add library. Then choose Next, or Continue once they're added. Choose a whole drive or your home folder and it warns you: reading all of it takes hours. The guide adds one library of each kind; more, and home videos, are in Settings › Libraries. Who's watching? Add a profile for each person in the house, or choose Skip. Added someone by mistake? Choose the ✕ on their picture. See Profiles. Watch on all your devices. Each app is listed with where to get it. Open it at home, and when it asks to connect, choose Allow. See Connect your devices. Watch away from home. Turn on Tailscale, and Disconnect to turn it off again. Not installed yet? Get Tailscale opens its download page: install it on the server, sign in, then choose Check again. In Docker, see Watch away from home for other ways. At the end, the guide shows what's set up, says Checking your libraries while it reads your files for the first time, and warns you if a library came up empty or Flexarr can't see one of an app's folders. If you leave part way, Home lists what's left under Finish setting up. Each one opens the right page in Settings; Hide puts the list away. Everything in the guide is in Settings too, as described below. You're signed in as the server's main profile, the one that can change settings. #Add your libraries A library is a set of folders holding one kind of media. Go to Settings › Libraries and choose Add library. Pick the Kind: Films, TV shows, Music, Home videos (videos of your own, arranged by folder; see Without Sonarr and Radarr) or, in the next release, Audiobooks (see Audiobooks). Give it a Name if you like. Left blank, it's named after its kind. You can rename it later. Under Folders, browse the server's disks and choose Use this folder on the folder that holds that media. Add more than one folder if your films are spread across drives. Choose Add library. The setup guide does this for you; this is how to add one later. Add one library for each kind of media you have. Keep films and TV shows in separate folders: Flexarr expects a films folder to hold films and a TV folder to hold shows. You can have more than one library of a kind, such as TV and Anime, or Films and Films in 4K. Home still shows one Latest unwatched row for all your films and one for all your shows, and a title that's in two libraries shows once. To give each library its own row, turn off Combine libraries of the same kind in Settings › Home & browse. Important The folder browser shows the disks as the server sees them. In Docker, that means the paths inside the container, such as /data/media/movies, not the paths on your NAS. If you can't find your media, check the volumes you gave the container in your install guide. #Podcasts are built in You don't need to add a podcasts library. There's always one, listed under Podcasts at the bottom of Settings › Libraries. Its Episodes folder is where episodes wait on their way to phones; you can move it with Change. See Podcasts. #The first scan Adding a library starts a scan straight away. You'll see its progress in Settings › Libraries, and titles appear on Home and in the sidebar as they're found. How long it takes depends on the size of your library and how fast the disks are, and artwork keeps arriving for a while after the files are found. You can start watching as soon as something shows up. After that, Flexarr rescans every 12 hours, and straight away whenever Sonarr, Radarr or Lidarr tell it about a new download. Each library has buttons to scan it now, refresh its artwork and details, rename it or remove it. Removing a library never deletes your files. Tip Films and TV shows get their artwork and details through Radarr and Sonarr. If you run them, connect them next. Without them, films and episodes still play, named from their files, with artwork and details from any .nfo files and images (poster.jpg, fanart.jpg) beside them, from TVmaze for shows, and from TMDB for films if you add a free key. See Without Sonarr and Radarr. Music reads the tags and cover images in your files, and Lidarr adds more. #The API key Flexarr still has an API key. You won't need it for everyday use at home, but it's there for: signing in another browser, or an app away from home when you don't use Tailscale scripts, Home Assistant and assistants getting back in if you've lost every signed-in browser Signed in as the main profile, you can see it in Settings › Security under API key: choose the eye to show it (with the admin PIN). Make a new key replaces it if it's ever got out. It's also in the server's settings file, config.json, as apiKey: Installed with Where config.json is Docker (including Synology and Unraid) /config/config.json inside the container, which is the folder you mounted at /config macOS ~/.flexarr/data/config.json Important Anyone with the API key can manage your server. Don't post it in screenshots or bug reports. #Next steps Connect your devices: your iPhone, iPad, Apple TV and other browsers Connect Sonarr, Radarr, Lidarr and Seerr Profiles for everyone in the house

title: Without Sonarr and Radarr
description: Artwork and details for films and shows that Sonarr and Radarr don't manage, from the files beside them, TVmaze and TMDB, and home video libraries.
headings: Artwork and .nfo files in your folders
text: Flexarr works best alongside Sonarr and Radarr, but it doesn't need them. Films and shows they don't manage, or every film and show if you don't run them, get their artwork and details in three ways, best first: What's in their folders. A .nfo file and artwork beside a film or show always win, even over Sonarr's and Radarr's. TVmaze, for shows. It needs no account or key. TMDB, for films, with a free key of your own. Anything none of these find still plays, named from its folder and files. #Artwork and .nfo files in your folders If you've used Kodi, Jellyfin, Emby, Plex or tinyMediaManager, your folders may already hold everything Flexarr needs. Flexarr reads: What Where Details (title, year, plot, genres, rating, age rating, IDs) movie.nfo (or Film name.nfo) beside a film, tvshow.nfo in a show's folder, Episode name.nfo beside an episode Poster poster.jpg, folder.jpg or cover.jpg Background fanart.jpg, backdrop.jpg or background.jpg Logo clearlogo.png or logo.png Season poster season01-poster.jpg (or season-specials-poster.jpg) in the show's folder, or poster.jpg in the season's folder Episode still Episode name-thumb.jpg or Episode name.jpg beside the episode A film on its own in the library's folder, rather than in a folder of its own, uses the same names with its file name in front: Heat (1995)-poster.jpg, Heat (1995)-fanart.jpg. Images can be JPEG, PNG or WebP. Flexarr only reads these files: it never writes or changes anything in your media folders. Tip The IDs in a .nfo file (TMDB, IMDb or TheTVDB) help Flexarr find exactly the right title, in Sonarr and Radarr as well as online. A .nfo that holds only a link to the title's IMDb or TMDB page works too. #Shows from TVmaze Shows Sonarr doesn't know are looked up on TVmaze, by the show's folder name (and its IDs, when there are any). They get a poster, background, overview, genres, rating and cast, with episode titles, descriptions and stills. There's nothing to set up. #Films from TMDB For films Radarr doesn't know, Flexarr can ask TMDB, using a key of your own: Sign up at themoviedb.org (it's free) and open Settings › API. Ask for a key. TMDB asks you to register an application first; that's the form for everyone, not something only developers do: Choose personal (non-commercial) use. Application name: something like Flexarr at home. Application URL: your Flexarr's address, or https://flexarr.io. Application summary: something like My own media server, showing details and artwork for films I own. Fill in your contact details and accept the terms. The key appears straight away. In Flexarr, open Settings › Connections, choose Connect on TMDB, and paste the API key or the API read access token. Choose Test, then Connect. Films that weren't matched are looked up again straight away. They get a poster, background, logo, overview, genres, age rating, rating, trailer and cast. #When the match is wrong A title search can pick the wrong one: a remake, or an older show of the same name. Titles matched by searching are listed under Check these matches in Library health. To choose the right one, open the title, choose Fix match… in its ⋯ menu, and search. Without Sonarr and Radarr, the search is TVmaze's (shows) or TMDB's (films), and your choice is kept in Flexarr through every refresh. Fixing a film's match without Radarr needs a TMDB key. #Home videos For videos of your own, add a library of the kind Home videos in Settings › Libraries. Nothing in it is looked up online. Flexarr arranges it by folder: Each folder in the library's folder is shown like a show. The folders inside that are its seasons, named after the folders. Any folders deeper down are part of the season they're in. Each video is an episode, named after its file. Folders and videos are in name order, with numbers counted as numbers, so Part 2 comes before Part 10. Name them by date (2019-07 Cornwall) to keep them in date order. Videos straight in a show's folder come first, and videos straight in the library's folder make a show named after the library's folder. Each video gets a still from a little way in. A poster.jpg or folder.jpg in a folder, or a -thumb.jpg beside a video, is used instead, and a folder without a poster shows its first video's still.

title: Connect your devices
description: Connect an iPhone, iPad, Apple TV or another browser to your Flexarr server with a short code, and manage the devices signed in to it.
headings: If the app can't find your server
text: Every device signs in to your server with a code. The device shows the code, and you allow it: on an iPhone that's already signed in to Flexarr as the main profile, which asks you by itself, or on the computer where you set up Flexarr. Each device then gets a sign-in of its own, which you can rename or sign out at any time. #Allow it from your phone When a device asks to connect, every iPhone signed in as the main profile asks Connect “Living room”?, with the device's code. Check the code matches the one on the device's screen and tap Allow. If settings are locked, Allow asks for the admin PIN first. If the device isn't yours, tap Don't allow: the device says Not allowed, and asks again only if someone there chooses Try again. The phone asks while Flexarr is open on it. When it isn't, a notification says the device wants to connect, if notifications are turned on for that phone. Tap it to get the same question in the app, or press and hold it: Allow opens the app to allow it there, and Don't allow answers without opening it (the phone asks to be unlocked first). The web app asks too, when it's open on the main profile. To see every device waiting, open Settings in the app, or Settings › Security › Connect a device on the web. Each one has Allow and Don't allow. Turned a device away by mistake? Choose Try again on the device, and allow it this time. (An app from before version 0.56 shows a new code by itself instead; you aren't asked about that one, but it's listed in Settings as turned away, with Allow.) #iPhone and iPad Get the app from the App Store. The first time you open it, three short cards explain what Flexarr is, that it plays from your own Flexarr server at home, and how it finds that server on your Wi-Fi. If you haven't set up a server yet, Set up at flexarr.io brings you to this guide. If you have, choose Skip, or Next through to Find my server. When iOS asks whether Flexarr can find devices on your local network, choose Allow. Without it, the app can't see your server. Under Servers on your network, choose your server. The app shows Connect this iPhone (or iPad) with a code of six letters and numbers, like H7KM2P. On another phone signed in to Flexarr, tap Allow when it asks (see Allow it from your phone). Or, on your computer, open the server's address in a browser, go to Settings › Security › Connect a device, type in the code and choose Continue. Check that the code matches the one on your phone, and choose Allow. The app moves on by itself a moment later. If your household has several profiles, it asks who's watching. If Safari on the same phone is already signed in to Flexarr, Approve in Safari instead opens the approval page there, so you don't need the computer. #Apple TV The Apple TV app isn't on the App Store yet. Until it is, install it with Xcode. Open Flexarr on the Apple TV. It lists Servers on your network; choose yours. The TV shows Connect this Apple TV and a code. On your phone, tap Allow when it asks, checking the code matches. Or, on your computer, go to Settings › Security › Connect a device, type in the code, then choose Continue and Allow. The TV also shows a QR code. Scan it with a phone that's already signed in to Flexarr in its browser, and the approval page opens with the code filled in. Note A code lasts as long as the device keeps showing it. If you go back and choose the server again, the device gets a new code. #Other browsers Browsers don't get a code. Open the server's address in the new browser and it asks for the API key: type it in once, and the browser gets a sign-in of its own, so it doesn't keep the key. The key is in Settings › Security on the browser you set up with (see The API key). Over Tailscale, browsers sign in by your Tailscale account instead, with no key. #Who can approve a device Only the main profile can connect devices. If the browser you're using is on another profile, the Connect a device page says so and offers Switch to the main profile (asking for its PIN, if it has one). When the approval page says the request didn't come from your home network, be careful: only allow it if your own device is showing that code and you started it a moment ago. If someone sent you a link to approve, choose Don't allow. #If the app can't find your server The apps find the server by asking the network for it. When Looking for Flexarr… doesn't turn into your server, work through these. #Same Wi-Fi The device and the server must be on the same network. Phones on mobile data, or on a guest network, can't see it. Many routers keep guest Wi-Fi apart from everything else on purpose, and some mesh systems and access points have a setting called client isolation or AP isolation that does the same on the main network. Connect to your main Wi-Fi, or turn isolation off. #Local network permission (iPhone and iPad) If you chose Don't Allow when iOS asked, the app can't look for servers. Open the iPhone's Settings › Privacy & Security › Local Network and turn Flexarr on. #Firewall The server's firewall must let other devices reach port 8383. On a Mac with the firewall turned on (System Settings › Network › Firewall), check it isn't blocking incoming connections. Check you can open http://<server>:8383 from another computer at home; if a browser can't reach it, the apps can't either. #Servers that don't announce themselves Flexarr announces itself to the network wherever it runs, but in Docker, including on a Synology or Unraid server, only when the container shares the computer's network. Docker's own network (the usual -p 8383:8383) doesn't pass the announcement on, so the app won't list the server. Run the container on the host's network (see Install with Docker), or enter the address instead (below). The announcement uses UDP port 5353 (mDNS). A firewall on the server needs to let it through as well as port 8383. #Enter an address instead Every app has Enter an address instead under the list of servers. iPhone and iPad: type the server's address, such as http://192.168.1.20:8383, and choose Connect. You get a code to approve, as above. Away from home, Connecting from outside your home? Use an API key asks for the API key instead. Apple TV: the same as iPhone: type the address and choose Connect to get a code, or Connecting from outside your home? Use an API key away from home. Use the server's IP address and port. You'll find the IP address in your router's list of devices, or on the server itself. #Manage and remove devices Signed in as the main profile, go to Settings › Security. Under Signed-in browsers and TVs you'll see every browser, iPhone, iPad and Apple TV with a sign-in of its own, and when it was last used. Rename gives a device a name you'll recognise. Sign out signs out one device. It'll need a new code to come back. Sign out every other browser and TV signs out everything but the browser you're using. If you think your API key has got out, Make a new key under API key replaces it, and can sign every other device out at the same time. Tip Each phone gets notifications for one profile, the one it was on when you turned them on. See Notifications and widgets.

title: Install the Apple TV app with Xcode
description: Build the Flexarr Apple TV app from source and install it on your own Apple TV with a Mac and Xcode, until it arrives on the App Store.
headings: 2. Sign Xcode in to your Apple ID
3. Pair the Apple TV with your Mac
xcodegen: command not found or go: command not found
Signing errors: "No Account for Team", "No profiles were found"
The app stopped opening after a week
text: The Flexarr Apple TV app is coming to the App Store. Until it's there, you can build it yourself and install it on your own Apple TV with a Mac. It takes about half an hour the first time, most of it downloading Xcode. If you only want Flexarr on an iPhone or iPad, you don't need any of this: that app is on the App Store. #What you need A Mac that can run Xcode 26 or later. Xcode 26 or later, free from the Mac App Store. Open it once after installing, and when it offers to download platforms, include tvOS. (If you skipped that, add it later in Xcode › Settings › Components.) XcodeGen, which makes the Xcode project from the files in the repository, and Go, which builds part of the app. With Homebrew: brew install xcodegen go. Git, to download the source. macOS offers to install it the first time you type git in Terminal. An Apple ID. A free one works. An Apple TV running tvOS 18.2 or later, on the same network as the Mac. Important With a free Apple ID, apps you install yourself stop opening after 7 days. Run the install command again to renew it for another week; your settings and sign-in are kept. A paid Apple Developer Program membership makes installs last a year. #1. Download the source In Terminal: git clone https://github.com/danleach-glitch/flexarr.git cd flexarr git checkout "$(git tag --list 'v*' --sort=-v:refname | head -1)" The last line picks the latest release, so the app matches the server you installed. #2. Sign Xcode in to your Apple ID Open Xcode, then Xcode › Settings › Accounts, choose + and sign in with your Apple ID. Xcode makes a free "Personal Team" for it. #Find your Team ID The install command needs your team's ID, a 10-character code like A1B2C3D4E5. Paid membership: it's on developer.apple.com/account under Membership details. Free Apple ID: Xcode makes a development certificate for you the first time it signs an app (or when you choose Manage Certificates… › + › Apple Development in Xcode › Settings › Accounts). The Team ID is the certificate's organisational unit. In Terminal: security find-certificate -c "Apple Development" -p | openssl x509 -noout -subject The Team ID is the value after OU=. #3. Pair the Apple TV with your Mac On the Apple TV, open Settings › Remotes and Devices › Remote App and Devices. Leave this screen open. On the Mac, in Xcode, open Window › Devices and Simulators (⇧⌘2). Your Apple TV appears under Discovered. Select it and choose Pair. Type the code the TV shows into Xcode. Pairing only happens once. Xcode may take a few minutes to get the Apple TV ready the first time. #4. Build and install Choose a bundle ID: a reverse-domain name that's yours, such as com.yourname.flexarr.tv. Apple needs every app's ID to be unique, so don't use one that belongs to someone else. Then, in the flexarr folder: make apple-install TEAM=A1B2C3D4E5 BUNDLE_ID=com.yourname.flexarr.tv This generates the Xcode project, builds the app, signs it with your team, installs it on the first paired Apple TV it finds and opens it. With more than one Apple TV, name the one you want with DEVICE= and its identifier, shown in Xcode's Devices and Simulators window: make apple-install TEAM=A1B2C3D4E5 BUNDLE_ID=com.yourname.flexarr.tv DEVICE=<identifier> The first build takes several minutes. When Flexarr opens on the TV, connect it to your server. #Updating the app Download the latest release and run the same command again: git fetch --tags git checkout "$(git tag --list 'v*' --sort=-v:refname | head -1)" make apple-install TEAM=A1B2C3D4E5 BUNDLE_ID=com.yourname.flexarr.tv Use the same bundle ID every time, so the TV treats it as the same app and keeps your sign-in. Keeping the app and the server on the same version avoids surprises; see Updating. #Troubleshooting #"No paired Apple TV found" The Mac can't see a paired Apple TV. Check both are on the same network, the Apple TV is awake, and it's listed (and connected) in Xcode's Devices and Simulators window. If it's listed but greyed out, wake the TV and wait a minute. #xcodegen: command not found or go: command not found Install what's missing (brew install xcodegen go), then open a new Terminal window. #Signing errors: "No Account for Team", "No profiles were found" Check the TEAM value is your Team ID, not your email address or name, and that Xcode is signed in to that Apple ID. Choose a different BUNDLE_ID if Xcode says the identifier isn't available. Someone else has it. #The app stopped opening after a week That's the 7-day limit on free Apple IDs. Run make apple-install again. #tvOS platform or SDK missing Open Xcode › Settings › Components and download tvOS.

title: Updating Flexarr
description: How to update the Flexarr server in Docker or on a Mac, what happens to your data when you do, and how to keep the apps up to date.
headings: Keeping the apps up to date
text: Updating Flexarr replaces the program and leaves your data alone. Your settings, profiles, watch history and libraries live in the data folder (/config in Docker, ~/.flexarr/data on a Mac), which an update never overwrites. #Before you update Read what's changed. Every release is listed, newest first, in: Settings › About on your server, under What's new the changelog GitHub releases Settings › Updates shows the version you're running now and the newest release, with what's changed in it. #Settings › Updates Flexarr asks GitHub once a day whether there's a newer release, and Settings shows a dot beside Updates when there is. To look straight away, choose Check for updates. The check sends nothing about your server but its version. What happens next depends on how you installed Flexarr: On a Mac (installed with the install script), choose Update now. Flexarr downloads the new version, checks it against the checksum published with the release, brings the .NET runtime up to date if it needs to, and restarts to install it, which takes a minute or two. If anything is playing, being watched live or recording, it asks first, because the restart interrupts it. In Docker, a container can't replace itself, so the page shows the commands to update it (see Docker below). Anything else, such as running from source, is updated the way you installed it. #Automatic updates on a Mac Turn on Install updates automatically to have a Mac install update itself. It's off unless you turn it on. Flexarr installs a new release between 4 and 5 in the morning, after the nightly backup, and only when nothing is playing, being watched live or recording. A busy night waits for the next. A release that failed to install isn't tried again by itself; you can still install it with Update now. #If an update doesn't start Before swapping in the new version, Flexarr copies the database aside. If the new version doesn't answer within five minutes, the version you had is put back, with the database as it was, and Settings › Updates says what happened. The update's own log is ~/.flexarr/logs/update.log, and the version that didn't start is kept in ~/.flexarr/app.failed so you can report what went wrong. The version before the last successful update is kept in ~/.flexarr/app.previous. Each update also brings the .NET runtime Flexarr runs on (in ~/.dotnet) up to its latest patch, as the install script does, so your server gets Microsoft's security fixes. The download is checked against the checksum Microsoft publishes. If it can't be fetched, the update carries on with the runtime you have, unless the new version needs a newer one. You don't need to make a backup by hand: Flexarr makes one itself whenever an update is about to change the database (see below). If you'd like an extra copy anyway, choose Back up now in Settings › Backup & restore. #Docker Flexarr's image is ghcr.io/danleach-glitch/flexarr. Updating means downloading the newer image and making a new container from it, with the same settings and folders as before. #With Docker Compose In the folder with your docker-compose.yml: docker compose pull flexarr docker compose up -d flexarr Compose replaces the container only if the image has changed. #With docker run Download the new image, remove the old container, and start a new one with the same command you used to install: docker pull ghcr.io/danleach-glitch/flexarr:latest docker stop flexarr docker rm flexarr docker run -d --name flexarr --restart unless-stopped \ -e PUID=1000 -e PGID=1000 \ -p 8383:8383 \ -v ~/flexarr/config:/config \ -v /path/to/media:/data/media \ ghcr.io/danleach-glitch/flexarr:latest Removing the container doesn't touch your data, as long as /config is a folder or volume you mounted. Use exactly the same options as before: the same -v paths, PUID and PGID, and --network host in place of -p 8383:8383 if you used it. Note On a Synology or Unraid server, use the platform's own way to update a container. See Install on a Synology NAS or Install on Unraid. #Which tag to use Images are published for every release with these tags: Tag What it follows latest The newest release. Every update you pull may be a bigger step. 0.57 The newest 0.57.x release: fixes, without moving to 0.58. 0.57.0 Exactly that release, never anything else. To have containers updated automatically, a tool such as Watchtower can pull new images and recreate them. Use latest to always get the newest Flexarr, or pin a version like 0.57 and change the number when you're ready to move on. Change the tag in your docker-compose.yml (image: ghcr.io/danleach-glitch/flexarr:0.57) or in your docker run command. Images are built for 64-bit Intel/AMD and 64-bit ARM, and Docker picks the right one for your machine. #On a Mac If you installed Flexarr natively on a Mac with the deploy script (see Install on a Mac), the easiest way is Update now in Settings › Updates. You can also update by checking out the newest release and running the same command again from the machine you deployed from: cd flexarr git fetch --tags git checkout "$(git tag --list 'v*' --sort=-v:refname | head -1)" make deploy DEPLOY_HOST=<your-mac> The script builds the new version, replaces the program in ~/.flexarr/app, brings the .NET runtime up to its latest patch, and restarts the server. It waits for the server to come back before saying it's done, and shows the end of the log if it doesn't. Your settings in ~/.flexarr/data are never touched. #What happens to your data When a new version starts for the first time, it updates the database to its new layout if it needs to. Before it does, it makes a pre-upgrade backup in your backups folder. The last three pre-upgrade backups are kept, alongside the nightly ones. You'll find them in Settings › Backup & restore. If an update goes wrong, install the version you had before, then restore its pre-upgrade backup from that page. See Backups. Important Don't try to run an older Flexarr on a database a newer one has already updated. Go back to the older version and restore the pre-upgrade backup instead. A backup made by a newer Flexarr is refused by an older one. Note If your backups folder is on a drive that isn't connected when you update, the pre-upgrade backup can't be made. Flexarr carries on starting rather than staying down, and says so in its log. #Keeping the apps up to date iPhone and iPad: the App Store updates Flexarr like any other app. To update by hand, open the App Store, tap your picture, and pull down to refresh the list of updates. Apple TV: until it's on the App Store, check out the latest release and run make apple-install again. See Install the Apple TV app with Xcode. Web: the web app comes with the server, so it's up to date as soon as the server is. Reload any open tabs. It's best to keep the server and the apps roughly in step. When a release adds something to both, the app's side of it only works once the server has it too.

title: Connect Sonarr, Radarr, Lidarr and Seerr
description: Add your *arr apps, Seerr, Bazarr and TMDB to Flexarr for artwork, Coming soon, requests and subtitles, with webhooks so new downloads appear straight away.
headings: Where to find each API key
Webhooks: new downloads appear straight away
text: Flexarr is built to sit alongside Sonarr, Radarr, Lidarr and Seerr. It doesn't download anything itself; it takes its artwork and details from them, and they tell it when something new arrives. If you don't run them yet, Flexarr still plays your files. See What you need for what you get with and without each one. #What each connection gives you App What Flexarr gets from it Radarr Titles, posters, backgrounds, overviews, genres, ratings and trailers for films. Upcoming films in Coming soon. Deleting a film from Flexarr goes through Radarr. Film series for collections. Sonarr Show and episode details and artwork. Upcoming episodes in Coming soon. Deleting a show or episode goes through Sonarr. Lidarr Artist pictures, album covers, canonical names and years, and albums, EPs and singles sorted apart. Readarr, Bookshelf or Chaptarr (in the next release) Audiobook details, covers and series, author photos and biographies, upcoming books in Coming soon, deleting books, and book requests. See Audiobooks. Seerr Discover and requests. Seerr, Overseerr and Jellyseerr all work. See Requests. Bazarr Search for subtitles from the player and a title's page, and re-syncing subtitles that are out of time. See Finding subtitles. TMDB Details, artwork and cast for films Radarr doesn't have, with a free key of your own. See Films from TMDB. Trakt Nothing to set up: Flexarr uses its own Trakt app. You can enter your own app's details here instead. See Trakt. Dispatcharr Live TV channels and their guide. See Live TV. Films and shows that Radarr or Sonarr don't manage are still looked up through their search, so a connected Radarr fills in artwork even for films it didn't download. #Add a connection You need two things for each app: its address and its API key. In Flexarr, go to Settings › Connections. Every app Flexarr works with is listed under Apps & Integrations. Find the one you want and choose Connect. Type its Address, such as http://192.168.1.20:7878. Paste its API key. Choose Test. A tick means Flexarr reached it; otherwise you'll see what went wrong. Choose Connect. Flexarr then adds its own webhook to Sonarr, Radarr, Lidarr and Readarr, so new downloads show up straight away (see Webhooks). Repeat for each app. Each one then shows a green dot, its version, and a link to open it. Choose the pencil to change it, or Disconnect in it to stop using it; its titles stay in your libraries. If you run more than one Sonarr, Radarr or Lidarr, such as a second Radarr for 4K films, choose + beside the one already connected and give the new one a Name of its own, such as "Radarr 4K". A second one has Remove in place of Disconnect. #The address Use the address Flexarr can reach the app on, with its port. The usual ports are: App Usual address Sonarr http://<host>:8989 Radarr http://<host>:7878 Lidarr http://<host>:8686 Readarr or Bookshelf http://<host>:8787 Chaptarr http://<host>:8789 Seerr http://<host>:5055 Bazarr http://<host>:6767 localhost only works if the app runs on the same machine as Flexarr and neither is in its own Docker container. Between containers, use the machine's IP address, or the container's name if they share a Docker network. #Where to find each API key App Where its API key is Sonarr Settings › General, under Security Radarr Settings › General, under Security Lidarr Settings › General, under Security Readarr, Bookshelf, Chaptarr Settings › General, under Security Seerr Settings › General Bazarr Settings › General, under Security #Seerr Choose Connect beside Seerr, type its Address and API key, and choose Connect. Once it's connected, Discover fills with what's trending and popular, and you can request what you don't have. See Requests. #Bazarr Choose Connect beside Bazarr, type its Address and API key, and choose Connect. Bazarr needs Sonarr and Radarr connected on its side, at least one languages profile and some subtitle sites (providers); set those up in Bazarr itself. A title you search for gets Bazarr's first languages profile if it has none, so Bazarr's own schedule may then fetch subtitles for it too. See Finding subtitles. #Webhooks: new downloads appear straight away Without webhooks, Flexarr finds new files on its own scan every 12 hours. With them, Sonarr, Radarr and Lidarr tell Flexarr the moment they import, upgrade, rename or delete something, and Flexarr rescans only that folder. Usually there's nothing to do: connecting an app adds a webhook called Flexarr to it, which you'll see under Settings › Connect in the app. If it isn't there, the app couldn't reach Flexarr at any address Flexarr tried: add it by hand. #Adding a webhook by hand The addresses to use are at the bottom of Settings › Connections, under Webhooks, already filled in with your server's address and its webhook secret. They look like this: http://<flexarr-host>:8383/api/v1/webhooks/sonarr?secret=<webhook-secret> http://<flexarr-host>:8383/api/v1/webhooks/radarr?secret=<webhook-secret> http://<flexarr-host>:8383/api/v1/webhooks/lidarr?secret=<webhook-secret> http://<flexarr-host>:8383/api/v1/webhooks/readarr?secret=<webhook-secret> Bookshelf and Chaptarr use the readarr address. The secret can only start scans, so you don't hand your API key to the *arr apps. In each app: Go to Settings › Connect, choose +, then Webhook. Give it a name, such as "Flexarr". Under triggers, turn on the ones for importing, upgrading, renaming and deleting files. Their names vary a little between apps and versions, such as On File Import, On File Upgrade, On Rename, and the Delete triggers. Adding a series, film or artist works too. Other triggers, such as On Grab or health events, are accepted and ignored. Paste the address for that app into Webhook URL. Leave Method as POST. Choose Test, then Save. Important The webhook addresses are built from the address you opened Flexarr on. If you're using it at localhost, the address won't work from another machine or container. Swap in the server's IP address or name. If the *arrs run in Docker on the same Mac as a native Flexarr, use host.docker.internal in place of the host name. Make a new secret replaces the webhook secret if it's ever got out. The *arr apps can't start scans until you give them the new addresses. #Paths must match When Sonarr says "I've imported /tv/Show/Season 1/episode.mkv", Flexarr has to find that same file. If the *arr apps and Flexarr see your media under different paths, as often happens with Docker, webhooks and some matching won't work. See Media paths to line them up. #Checking it works Settings › Connections shows each app's dot: green when Flexarr can reach it. Coming soon in the sidebar lists upcoming episodes and films from Sonarr and Radarr. Download something, and it should appear in Flexarr within a few seconds of the *arr importing it. If artwork is missing on titles that were already there before you connected Radarr or Sonarr, choose Refresh artwork and details on the library in Settings › Libraries.

title: Media paths
description: Why Flexarr needs to see your files at the same paths as Sonarr, Radarr, Lidarr and Readarr, how to line them up in Docker, and how to use path mappings when you can't.
headings: The best fix: the same paths everywhere
When the paths can't match: path mappings
Sonarr in Docker at /tv, Flexarr at /data/media/tv
*arrs in Docker on a Mac, Flexarr native
text: Sonarr, Radarr, Lidarr and (in the next release) Readarr talk to Flexarr about files by their path. When Sonarr imports an episode, its webhook says "I've just put a file in /tv/Some Show/Season 1", and Flexarr rescans that folder. When you delete a film, Flexarr works out whether Radarr manages it by comparing paths. If Flexarr sees the same file somewhere else, say /data/media/tv/Some Show/Season 1, it can't tell they're the same folder. This mostly matters in Docker, where each container sees your disks at whatever paths its volumes give it. There are two ways to fix it: give every container the same paths (best), or tell Flexarr how to translate them. #The best fix: the same paths everywhere Mount your media at the same path in every container. A common layout is one parent folder, /data/media, with a folder for each kind: services: flexarr: image: ghcr.io/danleach-glitch/flexarr:latest ports: ["8383:8383"] volumes: - /srv/flexarr:/config - /srv/media:/data/media sonarr: image: lscr.io/linuxserver/sonarr:latest volumes: - /srv/sonarr:/config - /srv/media:/data/media radarr: image: lscr.io/linuxserver/radarr:latest volumes: - /srv/radarr:/config - /srv/media:/data/media lidarr: image: lscr.io/linuxserver/lidarr:latest volumes: - /srv/lidarr:/config - /srv/media:/data/media The left side (/srv/media) is where the media is on the host. The right side (/data/media) is where every container sees it. Because the right side is the same everywhere, a file is /data/media/tv/Some Show/… to all of them. Then use those paths everywhere: Root folders in Sonarr, Radarr and Lidarr: /data/media/tv, /data/media/movies, /data/media/music Library folders in Flexarr's Settings › Libraries: the same three Tip If your downloads folder is on the same disk, mount the parent of both (for example /srv/data:/data, with media and downloads inside) in the *arrs. That lets them move files instead of copying them. Flexarr only needs to see the media. #When the paths can't match: path mappings Sometimes you can't change the volumes, or the *arrs run in Docker and Flexarr runs natively on a Mac. Then add a path mapping: "what Sonarr calls this, Flexarr calls that". #In Settings Go to Settings › Connections and find Media folders. Each root folder of a connected Sonarr, Radarr, Lidarr or Readarr has a line saying where it is on this server. Usually Flexarr works this out by itself. It compares the folders the apps keep their shows, films, artists and books in with the folders Flexarr found the same titles in. Sonarr's /tv/Severance (2022) and Flexarr's /data/media/tv/Severance (2022) mean /tv is /data/media/tv. When enough titles agree, Flexarr saves the mapping itself, on its next library scan, and the line goes green. When it's less sure, the line is amber: Use this saves the folder Flexarr suggests. Choose another or Choose folder lets you pick the folder on the server yourself. The app's line under Apps & Integrations also says when one of its folders isn't found, with Find it to jump to it. To write a mapping yourself, go to Path mappings at the bottom of Media folders and choose Edit mappings (or Add a mapping if there are none yet). In Path in the app, type the path the *arr app uses, such as /tv. In Path on this server, type where Flexarr sees the same folder, such as /data/media/tv. Add a mapping adds another line, and the bin takes one out. Then choose Save. Flexarr rescans your libraries straight away, and titles that weren't linked to the apps are matched again as the scan finishes. If you take out a mapping Flexarr saved itself, it doesn't add it back. #In config.json The same mappings are kept in the server's config.json (in /config in Docker, ~/.flexarr/data on a Mac) as pathMappings: { "pathMappings": [ { "from": "/tv", "to": "/data/media/tv" }, { "from": "/movies", "to": "/data/media/movies" } ] } from is the path in Sonarr, Radarr, Lidarr or Readarr; to is the path Flexarr sees. Leave the rest of the file as it is. Flexarr notices the change by itself; restart it if it doesn't seem to. #How mappings are applied A mapping covers its folder and everything inside it: /tv maps /tv/Some Show/Season 1/episode.mkv to /data/media/tv/Some Show/Season 1/episode.mkv. It matches whole folder names, so /tv doesn't match /tv4k. If more than one mapping fits, the longest one wins. You can map /data broadly and /data/4k somewhere else. Paths that no mapping covers are used as they are. #Worked examples #Sonarr in Docker at /tv, Flexarr at /data/media/tv Sonarr's container has -v /srv/media/tv:/tv, so its root folder is /tv. Flexarr's has -v /srv/media:/data/media, so its TV library is /data/media/tv. Path in the app Path on this server /tv /data/media/tv Or change Sonarr's volume to -v /srv/media:/data/media, set its root folder to /data/media/tv, and you won't need a mapping at all. #*arrs in Docker on a Mac, Flexarr native Sonarr and Radarr run in Docker Desktop with -v /Volumes/Media/data:/data. Flexarr runs on the Mac itself and sees the drive as /Volumes/Media/data. Path in the app Path on this server /data /Volumes/Media/data #Signs the paths don't match New downloads don't appear until the next scan. Webhooks arrive, but Flexarr can't find the folder they name, so nothing happens until its scheduled scan every 12 hours. Deleting a film or show offers to delete the files itself. The delete box says Radarr or Sonarr "doesn't manage" a title you know it does, because Flexarr couldn't match the paths. Importing your history from Plex matches fewer titles than expected, if Plex saw your files at other paths too. Albums don't pick up Lidarr's artwork, because Flexarr matches them to Lidarr by folder. To check, compare a file's path in the *arr app (on a title's Files tab, say) with its path in Flexarr, shown under each library's folders in Settings › Libraries. If the start of the path differs, add a mapping for that part. Note Path mappings only translate what the *arr apps and Plex tell Flexarr. Flexarr's own library folders must always be paths it can see.

title: Requests
description: Find films and shows you don't have yet, request them through Seerr from any of the apps, and choose which library they go to.
text: With Seerr connected, Flexarr can show you films and shows you don't have yet, and request them in one go. Seerr passes the request to Radarr or Sonarr, they download it, and it turns up in your library. Seerr, Overseerr and Jellyseerr all work. #Before you start Connect Seerr in Settings › Connections: under Apps & Integrations, choose Connect beside Seerr, type its Address (usually http://<host>:5055) and its API key (in Seerr, under Settings › General), and choose Connect. See Connect Sonarr, Radarr, Lidarr and Seerr. Seerr itself needs Radarr and Sonarr set up in its own settings, since it hands requests to them. Connect Sonarr and Radarr to Flexarr too, so requested titles show up the moment they're downloaded (see Webhooks). Note Seerr requests are for films and shows. In the next release, audiobooks can be requested through Readarr, Bookshelf or Chaptarr: see Audiobooks. Music isn't requested. #Where you can request Where Discover Request Web app Yes From Discover, its search and collections Apple TV Yes From Discover and its search iPhone and iPad No From Search #On the web Choose Discover in the sidebar. With Seerr connected, it starts with rows from Seerr: Trending this week Popular films Popular new shows Coming to cinemas Below them is Your library by genre, which is everything you already have. Each poster is marked if you already have it or it's already been asked for. For anything else, choose Request under the poster, or open it to see more about it first and choose Request there. #Search for anything The search box at the top of Discover, Search for any film or show, looks beyond your library. Type a title and you get every matching film and show, with the ones you already have marked. Request anything else from the results. #Missing films in a collection A film series collection lists the films you don't have under Not in your library, each with its own Request button. #On the Apple TV Discover is in the sidebar, above Search. It shows the same rows as the web: what's trending, popular films, popular new shows, and what's coming to cinemas. Select a title you don't have to open it. You'll see its ratings, cast, who made it, and more like it. Select Request. Press Menu to go back to Discover. A title you already have is marked with a gold play badge on its poster, and opens as itself. Search, at the top of Discover next to Browse, finds any film or show, not only what's in your library, so you can request it from there. Without Seerr connected, Discover on the Apple TV shows your library by genre, and says where to connect Seerr. #On iPhone and iPad With Seerr connected, Search looks beyond your library too. Films and shows you don't have are listed under Not in your library. Tap one and choose Request. Once it's asked for, it's marked Requested. #Who can request Any profile can request, with two exceptions. Kids profiles, and any profile with an age limit, can't request at all. A profile that can't see any of your film libraries can't request films, and one that can't see any TV libraries can't request shows. Libraries a profile sees are set in Settings › Profiles. Hidden libraries are left out of Discover and requests for that profile too. See Profiles. Flexarr sends every request to Seerr with its own API key. Seerr doesn't know which profile asked: it handles the request under the rules of the Seerr account that key belongs to, which decides whether it's approved automatically. Shows are requested with all their seasons. #Where requests go With two or more TV or film libraries Seerr can add to, the main profile chooses which one each profile's requests land in, by editing the profile in Settings › Profiles: New shows go to and New films go to. When two people have a TV library each, the shows each of them asks for go to their own. The choice applies to requests from every device. With one library of each kind there's nothing to choose. #Status and when it arrives A title's button changes to show where it stands: You see What it means Request Not in your library and not asked for. Requested Seerr has it. Radarr or Sonarr will download it when they find it. Partly in your library Some of it is here already, such as some seasons of a show. In your library You have it. Try again The request didn't go through, perhaps because it's already been requested. Flexarr remembers who asked for what.
